title: Spin counting via projection noise measurement of mesoscopic solid-state spin ensemble
authors: Lorenzo Bechelli, Konstantin Herb, Laura Alicia Völker, Christian L. Degen
abstract: Quantum projection noise is the fundamental noise source for the population measurement of spin ensembles. While projection-noise-limited measurements have been extensively studied in atomic systems, corresponding experiments on solid-state spin ensembles remain challenging due to dominant classical readout noise. Here, we report direct measurement of the quantum projection noise of mesoscopic ensembles of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) spin defects at room temperature. Our experiment is enabled by a high optically-detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) contrast of over 20% for a single crystallographic orientation of the defect spins, obtained by combining polarization-selective optical excitation with spin-to-charge conversion. We use our protocol to demonstrate projection noise measurements and spin counting from nanoscale NV ensembles of up to 43 spins. We further demonstrate that the protocol allows for significant gains in sensitivity for magnetometry applications without need for cryogenic operation or high bias magnetic fields.
summary: The research reports on measuring the quantum projection noise limit in mesoscopic ensembles of NV spin defects at room temperature. By implementing an advanced readout technique combining polarization control and spin-to-charge conversion, they achieved high contrast necessary to perform accurate spin counting up to 43 spins. This demonstrates a powerful, scalable platform for sensitive magnetometry without extreme operating conditions.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is measuring quantum projection noise (SQL) in mesoscopic solid-state spin ensembles, which is difficult due to overwhelming classical readout noise compared to atomic systems.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated direct measurement of quantum projection noise and performed spin counting on up to 43 spins at room temperature using NV centers. This protocol maintains high sensitivity without requiring cryogenic cooling or strong bias fields.
method: They combine polarization-selective optical excitation with a spin-to-charge conversion (SCC) readout scheme to achieve high ODMR contrast ($>20\%$), enabling the measurement of noise variance ($\epsilon_V(p)$) and subsequent extraction of projection noise.
model_or_system: The system is mesoscopic ensembles of Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) spin defects in diamond. The analysis involves modeling the total measured photon count variance, which combines fundamental quantum projection noise with measurable readout noise components.
key_observables: Quantum projection noise variance ($\epsilon_V^{	ext{proj}}$), ODMR contrast, Rabi oscillation decay, and the number of spins ($N$).
important_parameters: Room temperature operation; ensemble size up to $\sim 43$ spins; high readout contrast ($>20\%$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on separating the total measured variance into fundamental projection noise and measurable readout noise components, assuming controlled optical excitation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate spin counting concepts (Stern-Gerlach analogy), optimized ODMR spectra showing contrast enhancement via polarization control and SCC, Rabi oscillations demonstrating high contrast, and plots comparing measured vs. expected projection noise variance as a function of the driving angle $\phi$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the fundamental difficulty (readout noise) to presenting an advanced readout protocol using NV centers in diamond, demonstrating spin counting capability, quantifying the achieved sensitivity improvement, and finally discussing the broad applicability for magnetometry and sensing.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum optics/measurement theory with solid-state physics by providing a robust, room-temperature method to probe fundamental quantum noise limits (SQL) in a solid-state platform, which is highly relevant for developing practical quantum sensors.
